title: Help desk reports: The numbers that show where coordination breaks
summary: Learn which help desk reports matter most for B2B teams and how reporting improves visibility, service performance, and customer operations.
body_markdown:
Learn which help desk reports matter most for B2B teams and how reporting improves visibility, service performance, and customer operations.


You can’t improve what you can’t see. Front’s[Coordination Tax report](https://research.front.com/) found that only 5% of companies have a comprehensive view of handoffs, coordination time, and duplicate work. That lack of visibility is exactly why teams struggle to fix bottlenecks and service efficiency slips.


Help desk reports give teams the operational clarity they’re missing. Pull the key[customer service metrics](https://front.com/blog/customer-service-reports) into one place, and you can spot coordination failures before customers ever feel them.


This article outlines how to build effective[reporting dashboards](https://front.com/blog/customer-service-dashboard) and turn the insights into steady improvements across your customer operations.


## The right reports show where customer work slows down


Help desk reports matter because they show where customer conversations stall, not simply because they generate dashboards. Use them to understand how well teams coordinate work and where coordination breaks down.


For example, a logistics company could use its help desk analytics to watch how delayed-shipment inquiries flow from support to dispatch, warehouse operations, and carrier partners. Slow response or[resolution times](https://front.com/blog/time-to-resolution-metric-everything-customer-support-needs-to-know) at different stages highlight where handoffs or escalations create delays, telling you exactly where the workflow needs fixing.


## Measure the signals that keep customer operations moving


[Uber Freight](https://front.com/customer-stories/uber-freight) is a clear example of service desk reports driving real outcomes. The team was juggling communication across Outlook and Microsoft Teams with no reliable way to track efficiency. Consolidating everything into a single operations platform with detailed analytics revealed where work was stalling. Using those insights, along with automation and AI summaries, Uber Freight tightened its workflows and cut[response times](https://front.com/blog/first-response-time) by 50%.


Uber Freight’s gains started with visibility into the right signals. Broadly, those signals fall into four report types, each answering a question your operation needs a clear answer to.


### Workload and backlog reports


To scale well, you need to know how much work your team is dealing with and how that load shifts over time. Workload and backlog reports show both the volume coming in and how well the team keeps pace. Key insights:


-


**Conversation volume:** Track changes in the total conversation volume, whether it increases steadily or follows seasonal patterns.


-


**Ticket backlog:** Watch unresolved tickets to tell whether the backlog is shrinking, holding, or growing.


-


**Channel demand:** Identify which[communication channels](https://front.com/blog/customer-service-channels) customers prefer (email, live chat, Slack, or Teams) and how those preferences shift.


These insights sharpen staffing calls. Say a law firm’s support team sees inquiry volume rising and more customers moving from email to Slack. The team ramps up hiring and puts more reps on Slack conversations.


### Response, resolution, and SLA reports


These reports point straight to service performance — how fast teams respond, how efficiently they resolve, and where performance is slipping. Key metrics:


-


**First response time:** See how quickly teams give customers a first meaningful reply, beyond the auto-response.


-


**Resolution time:** Track[first contact resolution](https://front.com/glossary/first-contact-resolution) to gauge how often teams solve an issue on the first try. Average time to resolution shows how long it takes from start to finish.


-


**[Average handle time](https://front.com/blog/average-handle-time)** **:** Assess how much time reps spend actively working on each customer issue.


-


**SLA performance:** Monitor how consistently teams hit their SLA targets.


The goal here is to uncover where processes break down. A financial services firm, for instance, sees long resolution times on account approvals because gathering documentation and routing it to multiple teams for sign-off drags. The firm cuts the redundant approvals while still meeting regulatory requirements, and resolution times drop sharply.


### Ownership and workload distribution reports


These reports show how work is spread across the team so you can balance it. Focus on:


-


**Assignments:** See how many issues each team member owns.


-


**Unassigned items:** Look for any tasks without an owner. These signal gaps in the workflow.


-


**Utilization rate:** Monitor how much of each rep’s capacity is in use versus available. Compare across teams and people to find opportunities to redistribute.


Use these reports to keep work fairly distributed. A support manager notices some reps are consistently underwater while others have room to spare. They reassign tasks to even out the workload and update the automated routing rules so future work gets assigned by real-time availability.


### Customer outcome and recurring issue reports


These reports give you insight into the customer experience and reveal where recurring issues may undermine satisfaction. They usually surface:


-


**Customer satisfaction (CSAT):** Run automated surveys to find out how happy customers are with each interaction and get both[CSAT scores](https://front.com/glossary/what-is-csat) and qualitative feedback.


-


**Escalation trends:** Track the escalation rate across teams and issue types. Sudden increases may indicate training gaps or account-level issues.


-


**Repeat contacts:** Monitor how many tickets reopen after being marked resolved. A rising rate means fixes aren’t reaching the root cause.


-


**Recurring customer issues:** Look for questions and complaints that appear across multiple customers so you can either fix the problem or provide better self-service answers via an FAQ page or[knowledge base](https://front.com/blog/how-to-build-a-knowledge-base) .


Use these help desk metrics to turn scattered complaints into a signal you can act on. When a manufacturer sees repeated defect complaints traced to one production line, support can flag the product and operations teams to fix the root cause before more tickets land.


## How strong reporting helps improve customer operations


Front’s[Coordination Tax report](https://research.front.com/) found that 64% of companies experienced at least one customer-facing coordination failure in the past three months. These best practices for help desk metrics help you avoid those failures and run operations on reliable data.


### Spot operational friction before customers do


Frequently monitor your help desk reports to catch workflow bottlenecks before they affect customer relationships. Watch for sudden spikes in response or resolution times, and analyze those metrics alongside workload distribution and[escalation trends](https://front.com/blog/escalation-management) .


When slow responses coincide with a growing backlog in a particular team, you’ve found the source of friction and can take targeted action.


### Give every team the same operational picture


Reports shouldn’t live only with service desk managers. Use help desk software that gives every team real-time visibility into the dashboard as they work.


When teams see the full context, they make better decisions. For example, if they notice an agent is overloaded, they can redistribute work immediately. And if they see response times slowing for a particular account, they can prioritize that customer to[avoid missing SLA targets.](https://front.com/glossary/sla-compliance)


### Keep using reports to find better workflows


Treat help desk reports as part of an ongoing improvement loop, not static information. Even when you’re meeting targets, the data can point to ways to run leaner and[make operations more efficient.](https://front.com/blog/customer-service-operations)


If your workflows look efficient with no obvious bottlenecks, but reopened tickets stay high, it’s a sign that teams are closing tickets too early. Add a step to confirm CSAT before closing, and you cut repeat contacts and raise long-term resolution quality.

## FAQ


### How often should teams review help desk reports?


Teams should track[key performance indicators](https://front.com/blog/top-12-support-kpis-for-better-customer-service) in real time to catch operational problems quickly and make informed decisions. Conduct detailed monthly reviews to spot wider trends and longer-term opportunities.


### Can help desk reports improve SLA compliance?


Yes. By tracking[customer service analytics](https://front.com/blog/customer-service-analytics) via a real-time dashboard, you can see when response or resolution times are slipping and intervene before SLA targets are missed or you incur penalties.


### How do help desk reports support cross-functional collaboration?


Help desk reports give different teams a shared view of the same data, allowing them to fix workflow bottlenecks and coordinate work more efficiently.
